articles.title: Netanyahu may fall, but his far-right legacy in Israel is going nowhere
articles.summary: Israel’s far-right is accused of embedding a hardline agenda so deeply that reversing it may prove almost impossible.
articles.body:
As Israel’s opposition looks to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, speculation has centred on the possible fate of the current government’s more hardline, right-wing elements, including the parties led by the unapologetically pro-settler Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir , convicted of inciting terrorism.

While all members of Netanyahu’s cabinet, with the unflinching backing of the opposition politicians hoping to supplant them, have supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and attacks on regional states, it is Smotrich and Ben-Gvir who have been the focus of international attention and lightning rods for criticism by Western governments.

With talk of Netanyahu looking to form a unity government with Eisenkot, both ministers have publicly opposed a government led by the former chief of staff.

In the run-up to the vote, Ben-Gvir took the unusual step of claiming that Netanyahu now has a choice of selecting himself to “save Israel”, or Eisenkot.

Smotrich, meanwhile, has warned his ultra-Orthodox political allies against entering negotiations with Eisenkot, saying he will “dump them” once he uses their votes to oust Netanyahu.

Netanyahu formed a coalition government with Ben-Gvir’s far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) and Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party in 2022, giving both several of Israel’s most important cabinet positions. Smotrich became finance minister, granting him control over the Israeli budget and a number of institutions in the occupied West Bank, while Ben-Gvir was named national security minister.

Drawing on a wellspring of hardline Zionism, Jewish supremacy and what critics describe as unapologetic racism, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have exploited their political leverage to advance Israel’s most hardline policies over the past three years. They have also transformed their ministries to reflect their hardline ideological projects.

Both have been enthusiastic proponents of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, repeatedly threatening to withdraw their support from the government when it appeared Netanyahu might falter in the face of international pressure about the huge number of civilians killed, famine, and withholding of aid.

In September 2025 , Ben-Gvir threatened to bring down the government if Hamas remained in existence following the release of the captives under United States President Donald Trump’s proposed Gaza plan. Both ministers have repeatedly called for the annexation, settlement and ethnic cleansing of Gaza.

Smotrich has encouraged the expansion of illegal settlements within the West Bank and, in the eyes of his opponents, bears culpability for the explosion of settler violence and pogroms across the occupied territory.

In June 2025, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir were sanctioned by a wave of Western countries . Ireland and the Netherlands imposed travel bans on the two ministers, while other countries froze their assets. Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin said these measures were taken due to their shared “desire to see the elimination of Palestinians from Palestine”.

However, analysts said the ministers and their movements should not be treated as a homogeneous entity or be isolated from Israeli policy in general.

“I would argue that we should not treat Ben-Gvir and Smotrich as a single bloc, since exclusion from government would affect them in opposite ways,” Arie Perliger, of the University of Massachusetts Lowell, who has led studies into the far right in Israel, Europe and the US, told Al Jazeera. “Ben-Gvir’s power is populist and performative, and opposition suits him.”

Ben-Gvir’s roots in the outlawed Kahanist movement had, in tandem with many right-wing movements, relied upon their historical exclusion from power as evidence of a betrayal by the establishment, he added.

Smotrich, meanwhile, had used his position as finance minister to co-opt part of the settlement programme and force through his explicitly Zionist agenda. This means he would have more to lose if he were “cut off from budgets, portfolios and control over settlement policy”.

“Smotrich’s case is the reverse. His achievements were bureaucratic rather than rhetorical,” Perliger said.

Both figures have been accused of transforming their ministries in ways that will linger long after they leave government.

As part of the 2022 deal with Netanyahu that secured his finance portfolio, Smotrich was given the additional role as a minister in the Ministry of Defence. This gave him sweeping powers over much of the occupied West Bank’s Israeli-led civilian administration.

From there, he used his position to establish a separate Settlement Administration and to rapidly accelerate illegal settlement expansion across the occupied territory. In August 2025, he announced the revival of the E1 settlement plan , which he boasted would bury “the idea of a Palestinian state”.

Ben-Gvir has been accused of rapidly politicising the Israeli police force under his command and essentially fashioning it to mirror his own hard-right outlook. He has also introduced sweeping changes to the prison service, including severe restrictions on the conditions and rights of Palestinian prisoners, whose institutional legacy could last for years.

“These are personnel, procedures and facts on the ground and reversing them requires sustained political will,” Perliger added. He is sceptical that an opposition government would override the changes introduced by the ministers.

Ejecting the pair from the mainstream of Israeli politics was also unlikely to dent support for the groups, according to Roi Zur, an assistant professor in the Department of Government at Essex University.

Smotrich’s Religious Zionist movement goes back to the war of 1967 and, together with Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit, has the support of about 10 percent of the Israeli electorate.

“They are stable and will be there for many years … [They] cater to very similar kinds of people in Israel,” Zur told Al Jazeera.

Their lasting legacy may be the official sanction of hatred towards Palestinians which, long festering, exploded in the wake of the Hamas-led October 7 attacks. Through their actions, and those of other right-wing members of Netanyahu’s coalition, the value of Palestinian lives in the eyes of Israelis has sunk to unprecedented lows.

The widely publicised killing of more than 74,000 people in the genocidal war on Gaza, the willful neglect of Palestinian townships within Israel’s borders, where crime and murder have become a virtual epidemic, and the brutal conditions imposed on Palestinian prisoners have not been hidden so much as celebrated. Ben-Gvir was a leading figure in the passage through the Knesset of a death penalty law that solely targets Palestinians.

Meanwhile, the pogroms against Palestinians and their property across the occupied West Bank have continued without any meaningful government sanction.

“Violence is a constant danger,” said Aida Touma-Suleiman, the Palestinian former member of parliament for the left-wing Hadash party. “People are scared on the street, on the bus, everywhere. You have to be careful just to speak Arabic, wherever you are.”

Under the most recent Netanyahu government, apartheid against Palestinians, which had long existed in Israel, had become engrained and a version of fascism, Touma-Suleiman said.

“Apartheid is a series of laws that discriminate on the basis of race. Fascism is when the discrimination and the racism are carried in the soul,” she told Al Jazeera.

“Netanyahu and his allies haven’t just given permission to be racist; they’ve made it almost proof of patriotism – it’s expected.”

articles.title: King Charles jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
articles.summary: The monarch appears on a special episode to coincide with his 78th birthday on Saturday.
articles.body:
King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.

The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts.

"We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".

The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.

The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary.

"I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."

The pair selected a total of 14 tracks. King Charles picked Giant by Calvin Harris and Rag'n'Bone Man, telling Sir Elton that the song summed up his charity because of its message of finding strength from others.

Also selected was Bob Dylan's Gotta Serve Somebody, Muse's Feeling Good and Nectar Woode's Wine into Water, which features Sir Elton on piano.

The Rocket Man star asked the King to highlight a song that he found "extremely meaningful".

Replying that there is "nothing more meaningful than love", the King described an "unforgettable performance" of The Beatles' 1967 hit All You Need is Love by Sir Paul McCartney in 2002 at a concert in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Golden Jubilee.

"I shall never forget the magic of witnessing a simply unforgettable performance of All You Need Is Love for my late mother's Golden Jubilee at the Party At The Palace concert with Paul McCartney, Rod Stewart and Joe Cocker, and I think with Phil Collins on drums, Brian May and Eric Clapton on guitar and an all-star backing choir," the King said.

"It really is a totally timeless song with a timeless message."

The show opened with Tina Turner's hit Proud Mary. The King described the late pop icon as an "electrifying character" and recalled that the guard at Buckingham Palace played her hit Simply the Best following her death in 2023.

"It was, I hope, a small way of thanking her for the times she has performed for my charities and indeed for the joy she brought to millions of people," the King said.

The pair also chose Sir Rod Stewart's Handbags And Gladrags, Elvis Presley's Hound Dog, Pete Townsend's Let My Love Open The Door and Raye's Joy.

The programme will be rebroadcast on Apple Music One at 17:00 and 22:00 Saturday and again on Sunday at 02:00 and 06:00. It will also feature on Apple Music Hits on Sunday at 10:00 and 14:00.

articles.title: Device deemed ‘credible threat’ triggers evacuation around ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois
articles.summary: A suspicious device at an ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, triggered evacuations within a 1-mile radius, with local events forced to cancel as investigations continue.
articles.body: A suspicious device at an ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, triggered evacuations within a 1-mile radius, with local events forced to cancel as investigations continue. Police and federal authorities said early Saturday that they had found a device deemed a “credible threat” and rendered it safe, without giving details as to its nature. Searches were ongoing and the evacuation order remains in place, Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said at a press conference. “We’re going to have to search the entire property,” Dixon said, referring to the BioUrja ethanol plant. The area “has not been rendered safe,” he said. “There’s going to be an exhaustive search of the facility that has not been completed yet.” “I don’t want to get into how many we found, where we found them,” he added, but said those living in a 1-mile radius “should absolutely evacuate the area.” Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told NBC affiliate WEEK there was an “all hands on deck” response, saying: “A device has been identified. We know it’s a credible threat. We know it’s a bomb.” ​FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley told media that FBI personnel, along with local and state police, had determined a “suspicious package was a threat and rendered it safe.” Rep. Eric Sorensen, D-Ill., met with evacuees at Peoria Manual High School on Friday night. “This is the designated shelter area for those that are impacted by the evacuation that’s going on just south of downtown Peoria,” he said in an update. “What we do need to make sure is that everybody’s making good decisions. If you are within the 1-mile radius of the chemical plant BioUrja in Peoria, you have to evacuate.” Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker urged locals to “follow directions from law enforcement and stay clear of the area.” Country music singer Jon Pardi was forced to cancel his show scheduled for Friday evening at the Peoria Civic Center. “At the direction of the Chief of Police, tonight’s concert has been canceled due to an active local safety concern,” he posted on Instagram, adding that tickets would be refunded. Dozer Park, home of the minor league baseball team the Peoria Chiefs, also canceled a holiday event at the venue. The nearby OSF HealthCare St. Francis Medical Center said it was “taking all appropriate precautions in response to the situation in downtown Peoria.” A statement said: “We will continue to monitor the situation and take any additional steps necessary to maintain a safe environment for those we serve and those who work at our facilities.”

articles.title: 26 years in Britain, then a letter sending Nigerian woman to India: UK Home office's bizarre mix-up
articles.summary: A blind 67-year-old Nigerian woman who has spent 26 years building a life in Britain has been told by the country's Home office to return to India,
articles.body: A blind 67-year-old Nigerian woman who has spent 26 years building a life in Britain has been told by the country's Home office to return to India, despite never having visited the country.The extraordinary mix-up came in a letter rejecting her request for permanent residency, with the department suggesting she could seek treatment in a country she has no connection with. The decision could also leave her waiting another 20 years to secure the right to settle permanently in Britain.According to a report by The Guardian, the woman, identified as Comfort (name changed), arrived in Britain in 2000 and lost her eyesight shortly afterwards due to acute glaucoma. She was granted permission to remain in the country in 2022 under the long-residence immigration route after spending 20 years in Britain.However, with her permission to stay still requiring periodic renewal, her lawyers at Refugee and Migrant Justice approached the Home office seeking an exceptional grant of indefinite leave to remain (ILR), citing her age, disability and long-established life in Britain.The Home office rejected the request. In its refusal letter, the department initially said she could return to Nigeria, pointing to the availability of services for blind people there.But the concluding section of the same letter referred to India, stating that her circumstances did not demonstrate a lack of treatment in the country severe enough to warrant indefinite leave to remain.Comfort told The Guardian that she was devastated by the decision and the prospect of waiting another two decades for permanent residency."I’m very disheartened that I may now need to wait nearly 20 years to get indefinite leave to remain," she said."I have been living in this country for 26 years. I have found my home here and settled well. I have my friends, my church and do voluntary work. I’m a good citizen, not a law-breaker and am begging the Home office to have mercy on me and grant me indefinite leave to remain now, rather than making me wait 20 more years," she added.Questioning the reference to India, Comfort said she had never visited the country and had no connection with it.Nick Beales, head of campaigning at Refugee and Migrant Justice, who is supporting Comfort, criticised the Home Office's handling of the case and the government's immigration policy."This woman is blind, in her late 60s and has lived in the UK for a quarter of a century. She meets the rules to remain here and there is no public interest in making her continue to renew her visa," Beales told The Guardian.Comfort's case comes against the backdrop of a major overhaul of Britain's immigration settlement system announced by Home secretary Shabana Mahmood on November 2.The government has introduced an 'Earned Settlement' framework, under which migrants will have to demonstrate their contribution to British society, good character and integration before securing permanent residency.Under the existing system, many migrants can apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years of qualifying residence. The new framework increases the standard qualifying period to 10 years, while allowing certain categories of migrants to secure settlement sooner or requiring others to wait longer.The Home office has meanwhile told The Guardian that it was taking corrective action to issue Comfort an updated letter following the India-Nigeria mix-up.A department spokesperson said: "We do not routinely comment on individual cases. All applications for permission to stay in the UK are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the immigration rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant."The government estimates that more than 500,000 migrants could face longer waits for permanent residency under the new settlement framework.You use AI every day. articles.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after global outage
articles.summary: Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours.
articles.body: Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours. “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company said in an update on X. Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories. The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hourslong episode had impacted some of their operations. Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems started appearing around midday Thursday in the U.S. The company apologized on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents. It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change. The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech. “With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science. Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.” The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour. The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services. Microsoft scrambled to recover services A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents. Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer. As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks. For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send or receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday. Disruptions piled up from the courtroom to the pharmacy In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology. The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption. British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff’s office in Colorado’s Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected. Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies. “Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said. Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies. And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions. OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

articles.title: The world’s highest bridge is so much more than just an engineering marvel
articles.summary: In our roundup of travel stories this week: the world’s best cheese for 2026, the largest double bed in the skies, and the world’s highest bridge.
articles.body: In our roundup of travel stories this week: The world’s best cheese for 2026, the world’s highest bridge, plus a new feature: CNN Postcards. CNN is also following the FAA ground stop affecting flights. Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge The spectacular Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge towers 625 meters (2,051 feet) above southwestern China’s Beipan River, in one of the country’s most mountainous provinces, making it the world’s highest. Since opening last September, it’s not only slashed journey times across the canyon from roughly two hours to just minutes, but it’s transformed the region economically. Tourism is booming, with more than three million visitors turning out in its first year. Visitors can enter the structure itself, stepping onto glass observation platforms offering dizzying views of the canyon below. For those with even more adventurous tastes, there’s the bungee jump, along with an exposed walkway beneath the road. Guest accommodations, shops and cafés are popping up in the village below and new cellular base stations have been added to improve mobile phone coverage. Shopping mall secrets Istanbul’s Grand Bazaar is one of the world’s largest and oldest covered markets, dating back to the 15th century. Behind the vibrant and brightly lit world of the market floor, with up to 400,000 daily visitors, is a hidden network of craftspeople in tiny workshops who are masters of age-old techniques. Beating the bazaar in scale but not age, Shinsegae Centum City is the world’s largest department store, clocking in at 3.16 million square feet. And here at this mall in Busan, South Korea, visitors can enjoy a jjimjilbang, a uniquely Korean take on the spa experience. Meanwhile, the sprawling Mall of Asia on the edge of the South China Sea is one of the biggest shopping and entertainment complexes in the Philippines. It’s home to the newly opened Museo del Galeon, which tells the seafaring tales of the Manila galleons and the people that crewed them, and is an unexpected and tranquil respite. CNN Postcards: My first faux-pas A new feature debuts this week: CNN Postcards. Brief but vivid stories capturing the wonder, joy, humor or drama of travel: They flitted onto the jungle gym beside me — first one child, then two. We hung silently, like crows gathered in “The Birds.” I’d faced challenges on this, my first French camping trip, but handled them with the full courage of my seven years. An explorer in a strange land, I’d hammered tent pegs and said “merci” to the ice-cream man. Alien sounds shot out of the boy’s mouth. The little girl stared, waiting for my response. I leapt off and ran back to the safety of my family. My cheeks flared hot with deep, enduring shame. I wasn’t cosmopolitan yet. —Maureen O’Hare To read more CNN Postcards or to submit your own postcard-sized travel story, click here. The world’s best cheese Check the back of your cupboards. If you’ve got some dairy products that have been sitting there since 2024, you might well have the makings of a world-class product. A 24-month-aged Comté — a nutty, crumbly and deeply complex creation from France’s eastern border — has just claimed the top prize at this year’s World Cheese Awards in Spain. Farther south in France, Tony Shalhoub traveled to Marseille last year for his CNN series “Tony Shalhoub Breaking Bread.” There he explored his family’s immigration story, connecting with the city where his father had stopped en route from Beirut, Lebanon, to New York’s Ellis Island. CNN subscribers can watch here. Sinking the SS United States While the vessel is even larger than the Titanic, it took the SS United States mere hours to sink to the ocean floor in Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida. This once luxurious ship hosted presidents and celebrities and will now host turtles and fish as the world’s largest artificial reef. Subscribers can read about the ship here. In case you missed it The world’s longest and deepest underwater road tunnel is under construction. At its deepest, it’ll be more than 1,200 feet below sea level. Singapore Airlines launches “largest double bed in the skies.” It’s another hit for the “world’s best airline.” The best Brazilian beaches you’ve probably never heard of. Soft sand and unspoiled vistas. A tech shakeup. A midterm upset. A building collapse. What do you remember from the week that was?

articles.title: Restaurant chain may rethink controversial 20% service charge in some venues after customer pushback
articles.summary: A Ford's Garage franchisee in Florida is testing a 20% automatic service charge at select restaurants, but the company's president admits some diners don't want a mandated fee.
articles.body: Ford's Garage may be reconsidering a controversial policy that automatically adds a 20% service charge to customers' checks at select Florida restaurants, with the chain's president acknowledging that some diners are unhappy with the mandatory fee. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Billy Downs said the policy, which is being tested by one franchisee at five Florida locations, remains under review. "I think that we need to listen to the consumer on those things, to be honest with you," Downs said. "So, we are, and we may be encouraging a change to that program." RESTAURANT 'ADMIN' FEES SPARK BACKLASH AS DINERS QUESTION WHAT THEY'RE PAYING FOR Marc Brown, president of franchisee 23 Restaurant Services, told Fox News Digital the program has been largely successful, resulting in higher wages for employees without alienating most customers. "Our servers in the locations that run our service charge program are making significantly higher average hourly pay than our servers and bartenders in locations that do not have it," Brown said. The policy is part of a team service model introduced by 23 Restaurant Services, which operates Ford's Garage restaurants throughout Florida. Rather than relying on traditional tipping, the model automatically adds a 20% service charge to each check to support a commission-based compensation structure. Servers and bartenders earn commissions based on sales, while the model is also designed to provide more equitable compensation for kitchen and support staff, according to the franchisee's website. EX-WAITRESS REVEALS RESTAURANT TIPPING SECRET MOST CUSTOMERS DON'T REALIZE — EXPERT CALLS IT 'BAD HOSPITALITY' Additional tips are optional. Downs said the experiment was intended to explore whether a different compensation model could help control costs while rewarding employees for their service. "It certainly was a test to see if this can help keep the cost down to the consumer, as well as reward the server," he said. The Ford's Garage location in Plantation near Fort Lauderdale is among the restaurants that have implemented the policy "in lieu of a traditional gratuity," according to its website. That location also adds a separate 1% entertainment fee assessed by the shopping center. "This fee is passed directly to the retail center, is not a gratuity and is not retained by Ford's Garage or distributed to employees," the website states. APPLEBEE'S CUSTOMER PUSHES BACK ON SUGGESTED TIP AFTER CHECKING THE MATH Brown said the service charge is disclosed to customers multiple times verbally and in writing before they order, giving them the choice of whether to dine there. "So, to us, it's no different than just charging a higher price on the menu," he said. Most guests aren't bothered by the fee, Brown said, "because they like the Ford's Garage experience." But Downs acknowledged the policy has produced some controversy. "There's been some big wins, and there's been consumers that just do not want to pay a service charge," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The experiment comes as restaurant operators grapple with rising labor costs and changes to tipped minimum wages. "But the biggest pushback is people don't want to have a mandated service charge, and I get it," Downs said. "You know, I'm not sure I want it either in certain times." "We have not made any decisions, but we talk about it regularly." Brown, however, said the criticism appears to come from a relatively small percentage of diners, noting that most participating restaurants have experienced year-over-year growth after operating under the model for multiple years. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER He also rejected the notion that an automatic service charge diminishes a server or bartender's incentive to provide quality hospitality, saying employees are expected to "provide great service to every guest regardless of what they expect to get in terms of additional tip." Founded in Fort Myers in 2012, Ford's Garage has grown to 36 restaurants across nine states. Downs said the chain has prioritized affordability, with an average customer check of about $26 and weekday value meals starting at $10.99. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Downs, who previously spoke to Fox News Digital about the chain's emphasis on old-fashioned hospitality, said providing consistently good service can help address customer concerns. "If you give great service all the time, that can help to eliminate problems," Downs said. As for whether the service-charge policy could change, Brown said discussions are ongoing. articles.title: November planetary parade: How and when to spot it in the pre-dawn sky
articles.summary: The planets of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will align in pre-dawn sky throughout November.
articles.body:
Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.

Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.

Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.

From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky.

Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.

As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.

It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.

Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.

Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.

Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.

It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too.

It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.

Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.

Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.

Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter.

"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.

The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.

If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month.

At a similar time before sunrise, Uranus will be setting in the west. Then Saturn and Neptune will also be visible for a time in the evening rather than the morning sky.

What is the viewing forecast this weekend?

To view the parade, find a spot away from light pollution with a good view of the eastern horizon and let your eyes adjust to the dark for around twenty minutes.

The best time to view the planetary lineup is approximately 45-60 minutes before sunrise.

Saturday night will turn progressively more cloudy and windy with outbreaks of rain making their way eastwards.

An early frost could still be likely under clearer skies in the south and east, but even here the breeze and cloud will tend to increase.

Sunday night is forecast to be drier, as the day's rain and hill snow clear. However, wintry showers will pester northern Scotland with plenty of cloud.

Also the odd shower will pop up around north-west facing coasts.

Otherwise, the night looks mostly clear and dry, apart from the odd mist of fog patch.

Keep up with the weather where you are .

articles.title: Mamdani, Trump agree to 90-day delay in SNAP food stocking rules for US retailers
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and President Trump have agreed to a 90-day delay for small retailers to comply with new SNAP food stocking rules, ensuring that bodegas and corner stores can continue to serve communities in need.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has secured a 90-day extension for small retailers across the US to comply with revised food stocking requirements under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), following discussions with President Donald Trump and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins.The extension takes effect on Friday and gives bodegas, corner stores and other small retailers additional time to meet the US Department of Agriculture's updated requirements. Stores were originally expected to comply by November 4.Announcing the agreement on X, Mamdani said Trump had agreed to the extension after he raised concerns about the impact of the rules on small businesses."I spoke with President Trump and he agreed to give small business owners across America at least a 90-day extension to comply with new SNAP rules," he wrote."The concerns of the smallest businesses should always be raised to the highest levels of government."What do the new SNAP rules require retailers to stock?The revised USDA guidelines set minimum food stocking requirements for retailers participating in SNAP, which provides grocery assistance to eligible low-income households.Under the rules, stores must stock at least seven varieties of food in each of four staple categories: dairy, grains, protein, and fruits or vegetables. They must also offer perishable food items in at least three of these categories.The requirements affect retailers that accept SNAP benefits, including small neighbourhood shops that serve communities with limited access to larger grocery stores.Why did Mamdani seek an extension?Mamdani said the short deadline had raised concerns among small business owners and residents who depend on SNAP benefits to purchase groceries.Speaking at a press conference on Friday, he said the new requirements had created uncertainty for "more than a million New Yorkers" and "tens of millions more across America".He articles.title: Three killed in Russia as Ukraine claims US floated NATO membership option
articles.summary: Zelenskyy says the US asked for the first time whether Kyiv would cede land to Moscow in exchange for the NATO bid.
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone attack has killed a mother, father and their 24-month-old daughter at their home in Belgorod, a Russian region bordering Ukraine, according to Russian authorities.

The deadly attack came on Saturday in Proletarsky, about 20km (12 miles) from Ukraine’s border as Russia’s Ministry of Defence claimed the army intercepted 29 Ukrainian drones overnight, including several over the Moscow region.

In turn, Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched 96 drones from Friday evening, of which 81 were shot down or electronically suppressed as of early Saturday. It reported hits at eight locations and falling debris at two others, while a local power supplier reported outages in parts of northeastern Sumy.

Meanwhile, in Friday’s comments to reporters that were under embargo until Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said United States negotiators had asked during this week’s Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, the transatlantic military alliance.

Zelenskyy said the question had been raised for the first time but that no concrete offer existed. Zelenskyy maintained that Ukraine would not withdraw its troops but could put the issue to a referendum if Kyiv received firm security guarantees, funding for its armed forces and money for reconstruction.

Donbas comprises Donetsk and Luhansk, two eastern Ukrainian regions partly occupied by Russia.

Moscow demands a Ukrainian withdrawal from areas Kyiv still controls, while also opposing Ukraine joining NATO, whose members pledge to defend one another.

Zelenskyy said on Friday that he would not amend Ukraine’s constitution to make it neutral, arguing the move would not guarantee lasting security.

Ukraine has been defending itself, with Western assistance, against a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022.

This past week brought a resumption of US-mediated direct talks between the Russians and Ukrainians, which raised hopes of an early end to the war.

However, apart from renewed prisoner exchanges, there appears to have been little progress. European representatives are set to take part in the next round of talks.

Zelenskyy said the European Union and NATO are Europe’s “only real security” and that Moscow’s bid to review the continent’s security was “dangerous because … it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations”.

articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Montauk bikini designer's $50M yacht death lawsuit frozen as owner asks judge for exoneration
articles.summary: Christopher Durnan invoked maritime law to cap liability after Martha Nolan-O'Slatarra was found dead on a New York yacht at Montauk Yacht Club.
articles.body: The family of an Irish bikini designer found dead aboard a luxe yacht at a high-end New York marina is treading water after a federal judge put their state-level wrongful death lawsuit on hold while the boat's owner seeks exoneration or liability limited to less than 1% of their $50 million demand under maritime law. Martha Nolan-O'Slatarra was a 33-year-old Irish expat and New York fashion designer – whom police found dead on a 54-foot Sea Ray named "Ripple" at the Montauk Yacht Club in August 2025. The 61-year-old yacht owner Christopher Durnan, a multimillionaire insurance mogul and investor in the woman's summerwear business, has now turned to federal maritime law in a bid to avoid liability altogether — or cap his potential exposure at $476,942, which his attorneys said is the vessel's appraised value. "This is a typical delay tactic that is rarely successful and will not be here," said Michael Bowe, a New York attorney representing Nolan-O'Slatarra's family. "Mr. Durnan will soon have to answer to the complaint we are prepared to file and then to sit for his deposition." FAMILY OF BIKINI DESIGNER IN MONTAUK YACHT DEATH FILES $50M LAWSUIT ALLEGING ASSAULT James Mercante, an attorney for Durnan who specializes in maritime law, declined to comment. Filings like Durnan's are common, according to David Cattie, an attorney based in the U.S. Virgin Islands and another expert on federal maritime law. He said vessel owners have "vastly more protection" at sea than on land, if the facts of the case meet federal criteria. "But if they are claiming, and can prove, direct involvement or knowledge by the owner, those protections evaporate," he told Fox News Digital. "In short, he is asking the Court to invoke admiralty’s jurisdiction to stop the state court claims," he said. "He is also asking the Court for exoneration, [the] owner has no liability at all, or limitation, which caps liability and exposure to the value of the vessel post incident." The federal court battle will focus in part on what's known as "privity," he said — whether the circumstances that allegedly caused or contributed to Nolan-O'Slatarra's death involved something Durnan personally knew about or was responsible for. GABBY PETITO COURT BATTLE COULD DECIDE WHETHER CHARLIE KIRK FAMILY CAN PREVAIL IN UTAH WRONGFUL DEATH LAWSUIT "If the owner was involved in or knew of the defect that caused the harm, he cannot limit his liability to the value of the vessel," he said. Even though the boat was docked in the marina at the time, it was still legally in what's considered a "navigable waterway," Cattie added. "If the harm transpired on the vessel, it would be subject to Admiralty jurisdiction," Cattie told Fox News Digital. "If it happened on the dock and the deceased was moved to the vessel, it would probably not." WOMAN FOUND DEAD ON YACHT SPARKS SCRUTINY OF MONTAUK’S PARTY SCENE AND RISING WEALTH Durnan has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime, and his attorneys have denied any fault or neglect on his part. According to his federal court filing, Nolan-O'Slatarra was a guest aboard the Ripple on Aug. 4, 2025. Around midnight on Aug. 5, she was unconscious and unresponsive, and Durnan attempted to render aid, according to the filing. Durnan's lawyers wrote that he sought help from people aboard other vessels at the marina. One of them called 911 and another performed CPR on Nolan-O'Slatarra. "If any fault caused or contributed to the claims for loss, damage and/or fatality, which is denied, such fault, neglect, or want of care was occasioned and occurred without the Petitioner’s privity or knowledge," Durnan's lawyers wrote. "The Petitioner acted reasonably under the circumstances." Although the wrongful death lawsuit was filed in August, Durnan had not been served with it until Oct. 1, according to court filings. He had not authorized his attorney to accept service on his behalf and could not be found at his waterfront home on New York's Long Island, another one in nearby Garden City, where they saw a Lamborghini registered to his name, or a third in Windham, New York, about 150 miles from New York City, according to Bowe, who represents the designer's estate. Nolan-O'Slatarra's family faced a 120-day deadline to serve the lawsuit. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X A process server eventually found Durnan at a fourth property — his waterfront vacation home in Lantana, Florida, where they found a Rolls Royce parked outside, according to court records. After a days-long stakeout involving multiple process servers and private investigators, Durnan was finally served, allegedly telling one that he "was surprised it took you so long." The next day, Durnan turned to a federal judge with his petition to avoid or limit potential liability, court records show. "When we have trouble serving someone, it's a red flag that something fishy is going on," said Randolph Rice, a Maryland-based attorney and legal analyst. "Ultimately, this maritime maneuver may give the defense a legal lifeline, but it's far from clear whether the argument will float with the federal court." SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Durnan is invoking the same federal maritime law used by the owner of the cargo ship that struck Baltimore's Francis Scott Key Bridge in 2024 in an effort to limit its liability for the disaster, Rice said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB On Oct. 27, U.S. Magistrate Judge Gabriel W. Gorenstein approved Durnan's request to put up the appraised value of the boat as substitute collateral and ordered that related litigation "hereby are restrained, stayed and enjoined until the hearing and determination of this action." He also gave Nolan-O'Slatarra's family a chance to dispute Durnan's request. The judge set a Jan. 25, 2027, deadline for potential claimants to enter the federal case and challenge Durnan's bid. GOT A TIP? Town of East Hampton police arrived at the Montauk Yacht Club around midnight on Aug. 5, 2025, in response to a report of an unconscious woman aboard Durnan's boat. It was Nolan-O'Slatarra, who was pronounced dead at the scene. articles.title: The Trump administration is diverting billions in health funding away from low-income countries, defying Congress’ plans
articles.summary: The Trump administration plans to redirect or withhold nearly all funding that Congress had slated for international family planning aid this year – about $605 million – according to an internal US State Department budget report and a memo to lawmakers that were obtained by CNN.
articles.body: The Trump administration plans to redirect or withhold nearly all funding that Congress had slated for international family planning aid this year – about $605 million – according to an internal US State Department budget report and a memo to lawmakers that were obtained by CNN. The budget plans also involve an effort to move nearly a billion dollars into a global health innovation fund benefiting US corporations, while sharply cutting global health funding for low- and middle-income countries. The actions have drawn criticism from nonprofit organizations and lawmakers who argue it represents overreach by the administration, given that Congress holds the power to decide how money is spent. A copy of the budget report – called the preliminary Fiscal Year 2026 allocation – reveals plans to divert or repurpose almost all of the $607.5 million in funding that Congress had allocated to supply contraception and other reproductive health services to women overseas. Tens of millions of that funding will be diverted to support the “energy security needs” of US partners facing market disruptions amid the wars in Iran and Ukraine, according to a separate memo signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in September. The memo offered few additional details on how that money would be spent. For decades, US family planning aid has provided millions of women overseas with modern contraceptives to give them the ability to prevent or space out pregnancies, which research shows improves maternal mortality rates, family incomes and babies’ health. In fiscal year 2024 – before Trump came back to office – US investment in global family planning is estimated to have prevented 34,000 maternal deaths, according to the Guttmacher Institute. The budget plans also reveal steep reductions in US health assistance for most countries when compared to 2024 funding levels, according to an analysis of the leaked budget document conducted by Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy organization. Their analysis, which was shared exclusively with CNN ahead of its publication Saturday, was conducted in conjunction with the nonprofit organizations Partners In Health (PIH) and Population Action International (PAI), a reproductive rights advocacy organization. The countries with the largest funding decreases for health programs are South Africa, Tanzania and Zimbabwe, which have all been hit with more than $100 million in cuts. Eight countries – Afghanistan, Central African Republic, Gambia, South Africa, Somalia, Sudan, Timor-Leste and Yemen – have had their health funding cut to zero since 2024. Asked about the funding diversions, a State Department spokesman told CNN that “the administration is consistently evaluating the use of foreign assistance to ensure it is used to meet critical needs, including unanticipated contingencies such as the current global energy crisis, within the context of its annual appropriated budget and the authorities available to the president and the secretary.” Asked about the department’s diversions of family planning funding, the spokesman said: “Our focus is on implementing life-saving care, including in HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and maternal and child health, through new, landmark bilateral global health MOUs (memoranda of understanding).” Vincent Lin, associate director of health policy and advocacy at PIH, told CNN that the latest budget moves are “counter to what Congress has put in the appropriations bills.” “To see dollars that have been fought for and written into the law by Congress moved away or siphoned away to energy security needs, or to US private companies with a profit margin, or out of really important public health programs … I think it is devastating to see that happen,” Lin said. “The executive branch is flagrantly not spending the money that Congress has written into law for a very specific purpose,” Lin told CNN. “On the family planning side … this is the clearest situation of the executive branch ignoring and or violating the Congressional will.” In the last two years, the State Department has made several efforts to assume more control over US global health funding and make spending reductions, including by not transferring certain funds to the Centers for Disease Control. CNN has also previously reported on the administration’s redirection of $1.35 billion in funding intended for global health programs to cover the cost of closing the US Agency for International Development (USAID). Many of those changes have lacked public announcements or transparency. Public Citizen has sued the State Department in an effort to force the release of records surrounding those bilateral global health agreements, which the administration has largely kept confidential. That lawsuit is ongoing in federal court, but some of the documents have been released following Freedom of Information Act requests by watchdog groups. Congresswoman Lois Frankel (D-FL), who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, said: “The Trump administration’s refusal to spend Congressionally-appropriated funds for international family planning, as required by law, is shameful and dangerous.” “These decisions have real, life-changing consequences for women’s health, economic security, and opportunities, as well as the well-being of their families and communities,” Frankel said in a statement to CNN. Family planning aid diverted for ‘energy security needs’ In a memo to Congress signed by Secretary of State Rubio – which was obtained by CNN and first reported on by The New York Times – he said he authorized the redirection of up to $125 million in foreign aid to support “energy security needs.” More than $48 million of that would be taken from family planning aid, according to the memo. The memo also spelled out multi-million-dollar diversions away from other US programs, including peacebuilding initiatives between Palestinians and Israelis and overseas assistance for civilian victims of war. In the memo, Rubio invoked a law that allows the government to use existing foreign assistance funds to address unanticipated crises, saying that funding would be used to “support exigent energy security needs for partners facing coercive supply cutoffs, market disruptions, and inflated costs – particularly due to the deliberate, extortionary actions of Russia, China, and Iran.” It comes as the war in Iran has disrupted energy markets and led to a huge increase in global oil prices. The State Department memo didn’t give further details on how the money diverted for energy security would be spent. A Democratic Congressional aide told CNN the funding diversion is “an authority that they do have, but it is unlike it’s ever been used before.” Separately, the State Department budget document shows that another $32 million originally allocated for the United Nations Population Fund is also being diverted into other health programs. And a further $524 million in family planning aid is being withheld without a justification given, according to the analysis by Public Citizen, PIH and PAI. That funding is listed in the State Department budget document as “To Be Programmed.” Other publicly available budget documents list that sum as “unallocated,” which analysts said suggests the funds have not been made available for spending. “This decision is not consistent with the congressional history of bipartisan support for family planning and reproductive health care,” said Nabeeha Kazi Hutchins, president and chief executive of PAI. “It is Congress that holds the power of the purse, and the actions of this administration and the statements of this administration raise very serious concerns about whether the executive branch is exceeding its constitutional authority.” “For us, this is not just an isolated budgetary decision,” she told CNN. “This is part of a much broader policy direction that’s increasingly restricting women’s health and wellbeing.” It’s not the first time the Trump administration has indicated it does not plan to spend money on family planning or reproductive health aid, despite the bipartisan allocations made by Congress. Last year, Rubio said in his testimony before the House Committee on Appropriations that with regards to family planning programs, “we’re not going to be in that business globally.” The Trump administration has also previously conflated certain kinds of contraception with abortion – something that medical professionals have refuted. Shifting money into ‘innovation fund’ as foreign countries hit with aid cuts The 2026 budget document also showed plans to move $888 million of global health funding into an “innovation fund” that backs US companies working in science, technology and medicine. At the same time, more than $1.6 billion is being cut from global health funding for foreign countries, according to the analysis by Public Citizen, PIH and PAI. The move comes after the Trump administration last year launched an overhaul of the way the United States provides health assistance throughout the world, called the “America First Global Health Strategy.” The stated goal of the strategy is to have aid recipient countries further develop their own health systems – and the US decrease its assistance spending. But Public Citizen, PIH and PAI argue that in reality, the funding cuts and diversions are making it more difficult for countries to bolster their own health systems. “The administration’s cuts to country level programming takes away resources that support local health systems and services that deliver care and stop diseases from spreading. The simultaneous increase in resources for the innovation fund prioritizes commercial interests over these fundamental global health objectives,” the three organizations said in their analysis. The administration’s justification of the new “America first” strategy was that NGOs were wasting money and it should go directly to foreign governments instead, according to Peter Maybarduk, who directs Public Citizen’s initiative on access to medicines. “But the reality is, we’re going to take money from the governments and the NGOs and give it to big corporations,” he said. Public Citizen’s report also raised concerns about a lack of transparency regarding how government contracts will be awarded through the “innovation fund” of $888 million, which is far more money than when the fund was first created in 2025. The administration originally set aside $60 million for the innovation fund, according to FY 2025 budget documents. “The State Department has not clarified how it will solicit and review awards under the (innovation) fund,” wrote Public Citizen, PIH and PAI in their report, which also criticized the department for “increasingly relying on non-competitive sole-source awards.” The State Department spokesman told CNN: “The Trump administration is continuing to explore ways to identify and leverage American innovations to save lives, and to do so more cost-effectively while working with Congress.” The department did not respond to CNN’s question regarding the specific process for awarding contracts through the innovation fund. CNN has previously reported on the Trump administration’s use of no-bid contracts in other areas of government, particularly surrounding the renovation and construction projects in Washington, DC. There has been little public information about the specific projects and companies that the global health innovation fund will go towards. However, the State Department has recently announced some partnerships that it says promote American innovation, including contracts with the drone delivery company Zipline, the pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences and SC Johnson. “Without a transparent and accountable process for new awards, funding could flow not to those with the best proposals for public health impact, but to those with direct, private access to the administration,” the Public Citizen report said. “Moreover, new technologies are not a substitute for direct support to countries.”

articles.title: Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight
articles.summary: Milburn is not the first to try and fix the Neets problem - so what’s different this time round, asks Laura Kuenssberg.
articles.body:
It's an ugly acronym. And it's an even uglier situation.

The reality of so-called "Neets" in the UK - young people who haven't got jobs, aren't studying or being trained up - has seen hundreds upon hundreds of thousands in their late teens or early-20s struggle to find a decent future for well over a decade.

It costs the taxpayer billions. And the human cost is variously described as a disaster, a national shame, even a moral crisis.

When the phrase Neet was first coined by Tony Blair's Downing Street in 1999, the focus was on 170,000 or so teenagers who were not in education, employment or training. After many attempts at solving the problem, add in a pandemic and years of a sluggish economy, it's acute - with nearly a million under-25s in that situation.

A tome full of proposals to try and fix it once and for all will be published on Tuesday, after a year in the making.

How the government reacts will test its appetite and capacity for radical change, and the prime minister's real, not rhetorical, hunger for tricky political arguments.

The canny smooth talker behind the huge review, former Labour MP Alan Milburn, wants you to know that Andy Burnham knows exactly what's coming.

Speaking to me in Liverpool, where in Merseyside 14.5% of 16 to 24-year-olds are unemployed, he tells me: "All the way through, the prime minister, the chancellor, all the ministers, they know what's going on. It won't be a surprise to them when this is launched and that gives it a fighting chance of actually being implemented."

But his collection of proposals is not for the faint-hearted.

On top of a plan to stop under-25s claiming the main sickness and disability benefits, Milburn will argue for a dramatic shift in the balance of what the taxpayer spends on benefits for young people compared with what is spent on support to help them get into work.

He says the amount spent on young people's benefits is 25 times as much as that on employment support - and he wants to shift it to a drastically different two to one.

He won't put specific numbers on it yet, but accepts openly that means a significant number of young people losing their benefits or facing cuts.

But that would come with a chunky expansion of the amount of further education, training, health support and likely jobs subsidised by the taxpayer too. A big cut to state support on one side of the ledger, but a big increase on the other.

And to make sure that government gets really serious about improving the mess, Milburn is asking for a new law that would give young people a guarantee of help and support - a job, an apprenticeship, a training place, or perhaps health treatment so they are able to work - an "opportunity guarantee".

He told me he won't fall into the "elephant's trap", where a feisty teenager could sue the prime minister if they didn't get the job they fancied. But the idea is to put a legal duty on the authorities in a similar vein to councils' obligation to look after children in care, or to provide accommodation or advice to homeless people.

Westminster jargon often describes earnest sets of recommendations published in reports like this as "wide-ranging". This review genuinely is, arguing for changes not just in welfare, but in the health and education systems.

It's a real expansion of the state's involvement in the next generation, from one of the Blairites still standing, with the expensive Paul Smith knitwear to match.

He is not the first government veteran nor is Burnham the first PM, to try to sort out this problem.

But what Milburn and his allies say is different this time round is they're pushing for a whole new system that's permanent, not just another scheme that gets introduced by one secretary of state, then is dropped or scrapped by the next one that turns up.

And the notion of a legal guarantee is designed to make the state, likely through local councils or mayors, take responsibility for making sure young people have something useful to do when they emerge from school – for good.

The recommendations apply to the whole UK, but the precise way the powers might be used in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will be worked out when it gets to the finer details of draft laws.

The scale of the practical challenge can be seen from space. New research from the Lib Dems this weekend suggests that if nothing was done, the number of Neets would hit 1.26 million by 2031.

And Milburn himself cites figures that puts the cost of the issue at £22bn a year.

No politician would argue for the status quo. But agreement that something must be done doesn't automatically translate into consensus over what that something is.

For all Milburn's talk of grand ambition – his plans will not, any time soon, make much difference to the ballooning costs to welfare.

His plan will take as long as a decade before making a real dent in the benefits bill. And it will require taxpayers' cash at the start, although not the £6bn guesstimates that have done the rounds.

He's still coy about the upfront cost, but it will be billions over the years.

And he says plainly there are many young people who are capable of working but don't, although tiptoes carefully around any accusations that some take advantage of the system, saying he's convinced the vast majority of young people do want to work.

The Conservatives and Reform have both put saving tens of billions from the welfare bill, and fast, at the top of their list.

The Tories said Milburn was right that benefits must be cut - but that "unlike Labour, our plan goes to the root of the problem" including by halving employer National Insurance for young people and creating 100,000 new apprenticeships. Reform said the review "is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away" and it cannot be "another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."

Milburn and the government can expect sustained criticism that it's not acceptable the plans would take so long to start cutting the enormous bill for the taxpayer. There is no question the expected increases in benefit payments are absolutely eye-watering.

The opposition from that quarter, and indeed from the Greens on the left arguing already that what they have seen so far is "cruel", is entirely predictable to Downing Street. What's harder to read, and therefore more difficult to contend with, is how Labour MPs will respond.

Sir Keir Starmer tried, and painfully failed to make changes to welfare, sabotaging his own authority when he backed down in the face of backbenchers.

That's why Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, has spent hours and hours talking to Labour MPs in the last year, trying to patiently make the case for this plan.

And why Milburn, as he was keen to point out, has continually been in touch with No 10 and 11, trying to get Burnham on board even before he made it to Downing Street. A government source said hopefully, this time "we've done the ground work – it's not a rushed Treasury process driven by numbers".

As my colleague Iain Watson has written, the signs are healthier for Milburn, with a few key critics from last time showing more than an open mind to the new plans.

The political climate is completely different with Labour, for now, cheerier about the polls, and backbenchers reluctant to make trouble.

Burnham still is in possession of course, of the enormous majority that Starmer won.

There will, without doubt, be voices on the left of the party, concerned perhaps about opposition from the Greens or the SNP in their constituency who will never sign up to anything that would mean a cut to payments for anyone on benefits now.

"Look at the chaos Starmer got into," one source on the left warned, saying Burnham wouldn't be so "boneheaded" to do the same as "he wants to be everyone's friend".

So a possible fault line may become whether the reduced benefits apply to those already claiming, as Milburn believes, or only those in future.

A No 10 source is plain the plans would have to apply to those on benefits now, warning they must act as soon as they can, although new laws will take time.

They told me "an argument on welfare is an argument we are happy to have". Let's see if that sentiment stands the test of time.

The Milburn review was set on its path by Starmer. But it will emerge blinking into the light under a different leader, and in a very different political moment.

Perhaps, some in Labour wonder, Milburn's ideas are arriving at a time when a newish prime minister has big rhetoric but perhaps is short of big concrete ideas, mocked by his opponents for reportedly bringing in private consultants to fill out his much-vaunted 10-year plan.

Burnham is widely expected to adopt most of Milburn's genuinely radical ideas. Months of arguments lie ahead, however settled the political picture appears right now.

But Milburn's ideas just might have come around at the right time for a relatively new government . As one senior Labour figure believes: "You need some meat on the bones that isn't just, 'nationalise everything' – this could be it."

articles.title: Body found on French beach after attempted Channel crossing
articles.summary: The man was found after authorities stopped and overloaded dinghy leaving the beach overnight.
articles.body:
A man in his 20s has died following an attempted small boat crossing of the English channel, the French coastguard has reported.

Authorities said his body was found on Sainte-Cecile beach, near the coastal town of Le Touquet, on Saturday morning.

Overnight, a rescue team from France's Regional Operational Center for Surveillance (CROSS) had been deployed to monitor the boarding migrants onto a "makeshift vessel" at the beach, it said.

It reported that the vessel was stopped from departing by French authorities, and that no one was found in the water following a "thorough sweep".

Migrants using longer, more dangerous routes across Channel

The coastguard described the boarding process of the makeshift vessel as "chaotic", adding that five men were attended to by firefighters at the scene for signs of hypothermia.

A small craft was then deployed which - along with "land-based units" from the local fire and rescue service - conducted "a thorough sweep of the area but found no one in the water".

"Following the operation, at approximately 08:00 (09:00 GMT) the body of a man in his twenties was discovered on the beach," the coastguard reported.

It adds an investigation will be opened to "determine the circumstances surrounding the incident".

In the latest week of data, ending 8 November, the UK government reported that 903 migrants arrived by small boat into the UK in 14 boats.

A further 624 migrants were prevented from making the crossing, the data shows.

Earlier this year, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review after two boats carrying 21 people landed in Kent without being intercepted .

"Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare, but even one is one too many," she said at the time.

articles.title: US floated idea of Ukraine swapping land for NATO membership, Zelensky says
articles.summary: The US floated the idea of Ukraine ceding the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership during recent trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky says.
articles.body: The United States floated the idea of Ukraine ceding the eastern Donbas region to Russia in exchange for NATO membership during recent talks, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Zelensky told journalists that US negotiators had put the question and that it was the “first time” such a proposal has been raised. Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has long coveted the region, while he has cited possible NATO membership for Ukraine as a reason for launching his full-scale invasion in 2022. Much of the Donbas is controlled by Russia, although Moscow’s grinding ground offensive in the region has largely stalled. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” said Zelensky. He stressed that Ukraine would not give up territory but said if he received a “comprehensive security package” – which would include a strong Ukrainian army and guarantees from NATO and the European Union – he would put a proposal to the public. “If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not? I have no right to make that decision on my own. But we need specifics, and we don’t have them yet.” US-brokered peace talks between Ukraine and Russia took place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. The trilateral discussions were mediated by Trump administration envoys – US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff – and marked the first talks involving both parties in months, although they ended without a breakthrough. Kushner and Witkoff then went on to meet both Zelensky and Putin. Also in his comments to journalists on Friday, Zelensky questioned whether Elon Musk’s SpaceX was being honest about ongoing restrictions on Ukraine’s use of its Starshield system. According to Zelensky, restrictions persist along the front line and in Russian-occupied territories, impacting the operation of Ukrainian drones. SpaceX has denied imposing any new restrictions, after earlier restrictions to Ukraine’s access to the service were lifted in October. “The restrictions have now been in place for five days. They say it is some kind of technical issue. We do not believe that is the case,” Zelensky said. Zelensky also said that during the Abu Dhabi talks the US team wanted to discuss a new security framework for Europe, a notion he suggested was a ploy by Russia to shift the balance of power in Europe and the world. “I believe the Russians want to redistribute influence in Europe first and foremost,” he said. Zelensky has said that the idea of a new European security infrastructure could potentially be dangerous, and should only be discussed after first a ceasefire and then an end to Russia’s war with Ukraine is negotiated. The Ukrainian leader welcomed the agreement that future peace negotiations may now include representatives from European countries, a move announced by the US envoys although the Kremlin has not fully backed the idea. European involvement has been resisted by Moscow, meaning that for nearly two years, Europe – now Ukraine’s largest backer – had been effectively sidelined in the peace talks. “The main thing is that Europe will be there, and now Europe needs to decide and then agree with us on exactly who that will be,” Zelensky said.
